# The Keeper's Last Light

For thirty-one years, Elias Vane had climbed the same hundred and twelve iron steps every evening, his knees complaining at each landing, and he had never once counted them aloud. Counting was for people who expected to lose their place. He knew the tower the way he knew his own breathing.

The light on Gannet Rock had been automated the spring before last. A steel box now did what Elias had done: it watched the dusk, turned the great lens, and sent its beam across eleven miles of black water. The company had sent a letter thanking him for his service. It came with a clock, a small brass one, engraved with his name.

He still climbed the stairs every evening anyway.

Nobody had told him to stop, and nobody had told him to continue. The relief keeper, a young man named Tomas who came out on the supply boat every second Thursday, simply shrugged when Elias asked whether he minded the old man's visits. "Keep your own hours," Tomas had said. "I just check the oil and eat your biscuits."

So on the evening of the first storm of November, Elias climbed.

The wind had been building since noon, pushing the sea into long grey ridges that broke white against the rocks. Spray hit the lantern glass in handfuls. Elias stood in the gallery with his hands on the cold railing and watched the automated lamp sweep its arc across the water, steady and indifferent, doing exactly what he had taught it to do, though it had never needed him.

He thought about the nights he had spent up here in winters past, when the lamp had been his responsibility alone. He had trimmed wicks at three in the morning with frozen fingers. He had sat with a fever-struck fisherman's wife until the radio crackled and the lifeboat came. He had logged every ship that passed, every gale, every gull that flew too close and fell against the glass.

The logbook was in the cottage now, on the kitchen table, its last entry written in his careful hand: *Light functioning. Visibility good. Wind northwest, force six. All quiet.*

Below him, a single light flickered on the mainland, far off, where the harbour town was settling in for the night. Someone out there was rowing home. Someone was lying awake, listening to the storm and wondering whether the lights would hold.

Elias understood, finally, what the company's letter had not said. The light had never really needed him. It had needed the habit of him, the steady ritual that said *someone is watching*. Machines could turn a lens. They could not care whether a boat came home.

He stayed until the wind dropped, which was past midnight. Then he came down the hundred and twelve steps, one at a time, and walked home through the wet grass without a lantern. He did not need one. He knew the way.

Behind him, the light kept turning, and out on the black water, somewhere, a small boat turned toward it.
